passage: They call me "Mr Sincere" at work, and not kindly. I am Ramesh, and last quarter my team wanted to skip the final testing step to hit a release date. I said I would not sign off without it. "Too sincere," someone said. "Not practical," said another. It stung more than I let on, because I do like these people. So I made a joke of it: "Fine, put 'Mr Sincere' on my name plate." They laughed, and the room loosened. Then I stayed late and built a small script that ran the tests in a fraction of the time. Yamini, who had kept quiet, admitted afterwards, "I wasn't comfortable either." We are two now, and I try not to preach. Being practical and honest is possible, just slower to build.

qa.q: What nickname did Ramesh's colleagues give him?
qa.a: They call Ramesh "Mr Sincere" at work.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel when colleagues called Ramesh too sincere and not practical?
qa.a: It stung Ramesh more than was let on, because Ramesh likes these people. The hurt was hidden behind a joke while the line was held. 😅

qa.q: What could Ramesh do if the pressure to skip steps returns?
qa.a: Ramesh can keep holding the line with humour and skill, offer faster ways to do the proper step, and lean on allies like Yamini without preaching.

qa.q: How might Yamini have felt during the team's teasing?
qa.a: Yamini stayed quiet, and later admitted to not being comfortable either. Yamini may have feared standing against the group until Ramesh spoke first.

grounding: Colleagues mock the protagonist as too sincere for refusing shortcuts; he holds his line with humour and skill and finds an ally.

passage: The bank's loan desk was quieter than Vishal expected. Usha, the loan officer, pushed a thick form across the table, and his pen hung above the last page. It felt like a heavy stone hung round his neck. His chest was tight. He could sign, get it over, and stop feeling sick. Instead he said, "Could you explain how the interest works, what happens while I'm studying, and what I will have paid back in total?" Usha took out a printed sheet and walked him through it slowly. He asked whether he could take a little less than the maximum, since his hostel was cheap. "You can," she said. He took the form home to read once more with his father, and he felt afraid, but no longer blind.

qa.q: What did Vishal ask Usha to explain?
qa.a: He asked how the interest works, what happens while he is studying, and what he will have paid back in total.

qa.q: Why did Vishal feel as if a heavy stone hung round his neck?
qa.a: He was anxious that a big loan would weigh on his future, and part of him wanted to sign quickly to stop feeling sick.

qa.q: What could Vishal do before signing the form?
qa.a: He can read all the terms with his father, compare what he expects to earn from the course, and borrow only what he needs.

qa.q: How might Usha see Vishal's questions?
qa.a: Usha answered patiently with a printed sheet, so she seems to see them as sensible questions from someone about to sign a serious paper.

grounding: Signing an education loan feels like a stone on the future; the protagonist reads the terms, asks about the total, and borrows only what he needs.

passage: I am Hafsa, and I do not say this out loud often. When I got into engineering, my Ammi, Noor, mortgaged her gold bangles to pay my fees. She never asked me for anything back. But at family dinners she would say, "Those bangles are with the bank for you, remember," and I felt the weight of them every time. In my second semester I failed a paper. I hid it for a month, because how could I tell her? Finally I told Ammi. She was quiet, then held my hand and said, "I said it because I was scared, too." We made a plan together: extra tutorials, a proper timetable. I still feel the weight, but now I share it. Effort is how I honour those bangles.

qa.q: What did Noor mortgage to pay Hafsa's fees?
qa.a: Noor mortgaged her gold bangles.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa hide the failed paper for a month?
qa.a: Hafsa felt guilty under the weight of Ammi's sacrifice, so she could not bear to tell her about the failed paper.

qa.q: What could Hafsa do to keep the pressure manageable?
qa.a: She can keep the timetable and tutorials, tell Ammi honestly when things are hard, and talk about how the reminders feel. 🤍

qa.q: How might Noor have felt when she said the bangles were with the bank?
qa.a: Noor said she was scared too, so the reminder came from her worry about the future rather than from wanting to blame. It landed as pressure on Hafsa all the same.

grounding: Parents mortgaged jewellery for fees and remind her of it; the protagonist feels the weight, stops hiding failures and plans honestly with her mother.

passage: Chetan had borrowed a small sum from a phone app to pay his exam form fee. Cash arrived in minutes. Then the calls began. Threats, rude words, and messages sent to the contacts in his phone, calling him a thief. Every ring made his stomach drop. In a panic he took a second loan from another app to pay the first, and then the second began calling too. He sat on the steps of the bus stand in the kasba, feeling trapped. Leela didi, who worked at the Common Service Centre, saw his face and sat down. He told her everything. "Don't take one loan to pay another," she said. "Take screenshots of every call and message." Together they went to the police station and used the official complaint site. Chetan still felt shaky, but he no longer felt alone.

qa.q: Where did Chetan sit when Leela didi found him?
qa.a: He sat on the steps of the bus stand in the kasba.

qa.q: Why did Chetan take a second loan from another app?
qa.a: He was panicking and felt trapped, and hoped a second loan would stop the calls of the first.

qa.q: What could Chetan do next, besides the complaint?
qa.a: He can stop taking new loans, keep saving screenshots of the calls and messages, and keep his family or another trusted adult informed.

qa.q: How might Leela didi have seen Chetan's situation?
qa.a: Leela didi noticed his face, sat down and listened, so she seems to see a young person in trouble who needs support, not blame.

grounding: An instant loan app floods the protagonist with threats and shaming; he stops borrowing to repay, saves evidence and tells a trusted adult and uses official complaint channels.

passage: I am Jahnavi, and I share a hostel lounge with Akash. On Tuesday I watched his phone light up three times, showing the name Rohan. Each time Akash turned the phone face down and stared at the TV. I could not tell whether he was angry or embarrassed; his ears were red, that I noticed. The fourth time I said, "That's a lot of calls." He said quietly, "I borrowed some money from him. I can't pay all of it yet and I don't know what to say." I said, "Tell him honestly what you can pay and when." He stepped into the corridor and called back. When he came in, he let out a long breath. "He said thanks for telling him," Akash said, looking a little lighter.

qa.q: How many times did Akash's phone light up before Jahnavi spoke?
qa.a: It lit up three times, and Jahnavi spoke after the fourth.

qa.q: What might Akash have been feeling when he turned the phone face down, and how sure can Jahnavi be?
qa.a: He was probably embarrassed about the debt, as his red ears and his later words suggest. Jahnavi says she could not tell for sure whether it was anger or embarrassment.

qa.q: What could Akash do to keep the friendship steady?
qa.a: He can keep his word on the amount and date he promised Rohan, and tell Rohan early if anything changes.

qa.q: How might Rohan see Akash's missed calls and then his honest call?
qa.a: Rohan probably wondered about the silence, and thanked Akash for telling him, which suggests honesty mattered more to him than the delay.

grounding: The protagonist borrowed from a friend and dodges calls out of embarrassment, then calls back and tells him honestly what he can pay.

passage: Madhav had lent Shankar money before the semester started, and now Shankar ducked behind the canteen pillar whenever he saw him. Madhav felt used, and then awkward for feeling it. He rehearsed sharp lines on the walk home and threw them away. Two days later, at the stationery shop, he found Shankar looking at pens and said, "Hey. About the money. I do need it for my books. Can we fix a date that works for you?" Shankar's face went red. "I've been avoiding you, sorry. I was embarrassed. Could I give part now and the rest by the end of next month?" "That works," Madhav said. Walking back, he decided that from now on he would lend only what he could afford to lose, and call it a gift.

qa.q: Where did Madhav talk to Shankar about the money?
qa.a: He talked to Shankar at the stationery shop.

qa.q: Why did Madhav throw away the sharp lines he rehearsed?
qa.a: He felt used but also awkward about asking, and he realised that sharp lines would not solve the problem or help the friendship.

qa.q: What could Madhav do if Shankar misses the new date?
qa.a: He can remind Shankar kindly, ask again plainly, and remember that the amount may be lost, which is why he now lends only what he can afford to lose. 🙂

qa.q: How might Shankar have felt while ducking behind the pillar?
qa.a: Shankar was probably embarrassed about not being able to pay, which he admitted later. Avoiding Madhav seems to have made it harder for Shankar too.

grounding: A friend borrowed money and now avoids him; the protagonist asks plainly and kindly, agrees a date, and will treat future lending as a gift.

passage: I am Anjali, and for six months I told nobody about my credit card. My friends ate out often, travelled on weekends, and I did not want to be the one who said no. So I swiped, thinking I would sort it out next month. Then the statement came, and I sat on my bed staring at the total. I had been paying only the minimum, and the figure had grown. I felt ashamed, and I could not tell my parents. It was my cousin Joseph who noticed me flinch at a bill. I told him everything. He did not laugh. We wrote the whole figure down, I cut up my spending, and we made a plan to pay it off in steps. The shame was worse than the number.

qa.q: For how long had Anjali told nobody about her credit card?
qa.a: She told nobody for six months.

qa.q: Why did Anjali keep swiping instead of saying no to her friends?
qa.a: She did not want to be the one who said no to the group, so she hoped she would sort it out next month.

qa.q: What could Anjali do to stop it happening again?
qa.a: She can keep her spending within what she can pay, keep the written figure and repayment plan, and keep talking to Joseph or another safe person.

qa.q: How might Joseph have seen Anjali's confession?
qa.a: Joseph did not laugh and helped write down the whole figure, so he seems to see a cousin who needs help and a plan, not judgement.

grounding: The protagonist overspent on a credit card to keep up with friends and hid it; she totals the figure, stops spending, tells someone safe and makes a plan.

passage: I am Gargi, and I share a flat with Harsha. This is what I saw over two months. Harsha's rent was late, and when his uncle offered a short helping hand, Harsha said, "No thanks, I'm fine." He said it lightly, but he went quiet afterwards. A week later he told me a quick lender had given him money on the same day. The lender charged a lot, and I saw him doing sums on the back of a notebook and frowning. I can't say whether it was pride or worry; he only said, "I want to do this myself." By the third week he looked tired. One evening he picked up his phone, hesitated, and called his uncle. I heard him say, "Could I borrow until the first, and pay it back on that date?"

qa.q: Who did Harsha finally call one evening?
qa.a: Harsha called his uncle.

qa.q: What might Harsha have been feeling when he refused his uncle's help, and how sure can Gargi be?
qa.a: He may have felt pride in doing things on his own, though he went quiet afterwards. Gargi says she cannot say for sure whether it was pride or worry.

qa.q: What could Harsha do to stay independent without paying heavily?
qa.a: He can accept a short, clear bridge from family with a repayment date, and keep proud independence for the long run.

qa.q: How might Harsha's uncle have felt when the help was refused and then asked for?
qa.a: The uncle offered help, so he may have been a little hurt at first but probably glad to help when Harsha called, since he was willing all along.

grounding: The protagonist refuses relatives' help to look self-made and pays a lot to a lender, then asks his uncle for a short bridge with a date.

passage:
Dear Sarita,
I have to tell you what happened on Tuesday, and please tell your hostel friends too. A man called and said he was from my bank. He knew my full name, and said my account would be blocked within the hour unless I acted now. My hands went cold, and I thought of the money for my course fees. He asked for the code that had just arrived on my phone. I already had my thumb on it. Then I remembered what Papa always says: pause and check. I hung up. I called the number printed on my card, and the bank said they had made no such call. I never shared the code. My heart is still thumping while I write this.
Vijay

qa.q: What did the caller say would happen to Vijay's account?
qa.a: The caller said it would be blocked within the hour.

qa.q: What feelings did the caller use against Vijay, and how can you tell?
qa.a: The caller used fear of losing the account and money, and urgency. Vijay's cold hands and worry about course fees show it worked at first.

qa.q: What should Vijay do if he gets another call like this?
qa.a: He should hang up, verify through the number printed on his card or the bank's official channel, and never share codes with a caller.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel reading Vijay's letter?
qa.a: Sarita may feel alarmed but also grateful for the warning, since Vijay asks her to tell her hostel friends. It gives her a simple habit: pause and check.

grounding: A caller posing as a bank knew the protagonist's name and urged him to act now; he paused, hung up and verified through the official number.

passage:
Monday. Aparna paid a "registration fee" for a work-from-home job that promised a quick start, using most of her savings. By evening the messages stopped and the number was dead. She sat on her bed, feeling stupid and sick.
Tuesday. She told her brother Akash, expecting him to scold her. Instead he said, "They do this for a living. They aim at hope, not at stupid people." He sat beside her while she called the cyber helpline and reported everything, and later he told their parents with her.
The next Sunday. Aparna wrote in her college group what had happened and how the offer looked, so others could spot it. Two classmates thanked her. She still ached over the loss, but the shame had shrunk.

qa.q: Whom did Aparna tell on Tuesday?
qa.a: She told her brother Akash.

qa.q: Why did Aparna feel stupid on Monday evening?
qa.a: She had lost most of her savings to a fake job offer and blamed herself for falling for it.

qa.q: What steps did Aparna take that could help her and others?
qa.a: She reported it to the cyber helpline right away, told her family, and shared her story so other students could recognise the offer.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt when Aparna told him?
qa.a: Akash did not scold her, and said scammers aim at hope, not at stupid people. He seems to have felt protective and wanted to make her feel less alone. 🤍

grounding: The protagonist lost her savings to a fake job offer and feels stupid; she learns scams target hope, reports at once, tells family and warns others.
